meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Nature to be commanded must be obeyed'?
meta.ogDescription: Bacon really wrote it, in Latin, in 1620. The memorable English sentence belongs to his Victorian translator — plus the Henry Adams mix-up.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1561–1626 · English philosopher, statesman & Lord Chancellor of England
answer.sourceLine: Bacon wrote it — but in Latin. The sentence is Novum Organum (1620), Book I, Aphorism 3: “Natura enim non nisi parendo vincitur.” The familiar English wording is James Spedding’s, printed in The Works of Francis Bacon, vol. 4 ↗ at page 47, and Wikiquote files it in its sourced section at the same aphorism.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Book I, Aphorism 3 (of the Instauratio Magna, Part II)
James Spedding et al., in The Works of Francis Bacon, vol. 4 (London: Longmans, 1858), p. 47

source.excerpt: Human knowledge and human power meet in one; for where the cause is not known the effect cannot be produced. Nature to be commanded must be obeyed; and that which in contemplation is as the cause is in operation as the rule.
trail: Started with the specialists. Quote Investigator has no entry for this line, so the anchor is Wikiquote, which lists it in its sourced Novum Organum (1620) section ↗ and cites Book I, Aphorism 3.
Read the English text itself. The Spedding translation at Wikisource ↗ carries the sentence verbatim inside Aphorism III, and the page’s inline pagination puts it on p. 47 of volume 4.
Checked the Latin. The Latin text of Book I ↗ gives Aphorism III as Natura enim non nisi parendo vincitur — confirming Bacon wrote the thought, and that “commanded” is the translator’s word.

Tested the wording against a second translation. Joseph Devey’s 1902 edition ↗ renders the same clause “nature is only subdued by submission,” which is how we know the memorable phrasing is a translation choice rather than a fixed feature of the original.
source.excerptNote: Aphorism III in full, in the Spedding translation. Bacon’s Latin: Scientia et potentia humana in idem coincidunt, quia ignoratio causae destituit effectum. Natura enim non nisi parendo vincitur: et quod in contemplatione instar causae est, id in operatione instar regulae est.

sourceLink.text: Novum Organum, Book I (Spedding translation) at Wikisource

source.rightsNote: Both layers are clear. Bacon’s Latin Novum Organum was first published in 1620, and the exact English wording quoted here comes from the Spedding, Ellis and Heath edition of The Works of Francis Bacon, vol. 4, published in London in 1858 — well before the 1931 US copyright cutoff, so the translation is public domain in its own right. Quote it freely; a modern translation of the same aphorism would not be.

author.name: Francis Bacon
author.heading: Who was Francis Bacon?
author.metaLine: 1561–1626 · English philosopher, statesman & Lord Chancellor of England
author.bio: Francis Bacon climbed to Attorney General and then Lord Chancellor of England before falling from office in disgrace — but his lasting work was a demolition job on how people reasoned. Novum Organum (1620) argued that the unaided mind invents patterns nature never had, and that the only cure is patient, instrumented observation. He wrote it in Latin, as Part II of a vast unfinished project he called the Instauratio Magna, and it is the book that made him a pioneer of empirical scientific method.

misattribution.heading: What gets garbled
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Bacon is solid — unusually so for a line this quotable. What travels loose is the wording, and occasionally the messenger.

items.why: Bacon wrote in Latin: Natura enim non nisi parendo vincitur — nearer to “for nature is not conquered except by obeying” (Latin text ↗). The proverb-shaped English is Spedding’s. Joseph Devey’s 1902 translation renders the identical clause “nature is only subdued by submission ↗” — same Bacon, no proverb.

Goodreads credits “Nature, to be commanded, must be obeyed. The imagination must be given not wings but weights.” to Henry Adams, The Education of Henry Adams ↗. In Chapter XXXIII of that book ↗ Adams is plainly quoting someone else — the two sentences sit in quotation marks in a paragraph about “Lord Bacon.” Adams also prints commas round the middle clause; Spedding’s text has none, and the comma’d form is the one that circulates today.

“The imagination must be given not wings but weights” is not how the Spedding translation reads either. Bacon’s Aphorism CIV says the understanding — not the imagination — “must not therefore be supplied with wings, but rather hung with weights, to keep it from leaping and flying ↗.”

“We cannot command nature except by obeying her” is a genuinely different sentence, from a different part of Novum Organum — Wikiquote lists it separately at Aphorism 129 ↗, where the Latin runs Naturae enim non imperatur, nisi parendo. Quote sites regularly merge the two or swap one citation for the other.

misattribution.truthLine: Bacon wrote the thought, in Latin, in 1620. The English sentence everyone quotes is James Spedding’s rendering of Aphorism 3 ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Aphorism 3 sits three sentences into the book that tried to restart European thinking from scratch. Bacon’s claim is deliberately deflating: human knowledge and human power are the same thing, because you cannot make an effect happen until you know its cause. Mastery is not a matter of will. It is a matter of submission to how things actually work — and the aphorism ends by making the point twice over, since what functions as a cause in thought functions as a rule in practice.

That was an argument against the magicians and the schoolmen at once. The alchemist commanded nature by incantation; the scholastic deduced it from first principles. Bacon told both that the road ran the other way — observe first, obey what you find, and command follows. Everything in the book after this point is machinery for doing that obeying carefully.
detailsBody: The Latin is compressed almost to the point of rudeness: Natura enim non nisi parendo vincitur — literally, for nature is not conquered except by obeying. There is no “commanded” in it and no “must”; vincitur is the vocabulary of conquest, not of command.

Spedding’s “Nature to be commanded must be obeyed” is what turned a dense Latin clause into an English proverb — it balances, it scans, and it is short enough to carve into a lintel. How much of that is Bacon and how much is his Victorian translator is visible the moment you set another translation beside it: Joseph Devey’s 1902 version of the same sentence reads “for nature is only subdued by submission,” which nobody has ever quoted.
